stem: A 56-year-old woman develops progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and leg swelling 6 months after finishing chemotherapy with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide for breast cancer. Echocardiography shows dilated ventricles and an ejection fraction of 30%. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary edema.
oneliner: 56F + breast cancer treated with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide 6 mo ago + dyspnea, orthopnea, edema + EF 30% + cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema → mechanism of heart injury?
ask: Which of the following best explains her cardiac findings?

options.A: Blockade of fatty acid beta-oxidation in myocytes
options.B: Decreased oxidative phosphorylation from cytochrome inhibition
options.C: Free radical formation with lipid peroxidation of myocyte membranes
options.D: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in the heart
options.E: Blockade of HER2 signaling in myocytes

whyNot.A: Seen with **carnitine deficiency** or certain toxins, not anthracyclines
whyNot.B: A **cyanide-type** mitochondrial poison effect; not this drug
whyNot.D: Would cause **bradycardia and cholinergic signs**, not dilated cardiomyopathy
whyNot.E: **Trastuzumab** mechanism (usually reversible); she did not receive it

answer: Free radical lipid peroxidation of myocyte membranes (doxorubicin)
why: **Dilated cardiomyopathy months after breast cancer chemotherapy** points to **doxorubicin**: iron-linked **free radicals cause lipid peroxidation** of cardiomyocyte membranes. Dexrazoxane (iron chelator) protects the heart.

drug.name: Doxorubicin
drug.how: Intercalates DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II; generates free radicals
drug.use: Breast cancer, lymphomas, sarcomas, many solid tumors
drug.watch: Dilated cardiomyopathy (dose-related), myelosuppression, alopecia; dexrazoxane is cardioprotective

stem: A 24-year-old man with Hodgkin lymphoma has had a dry cough and exertional dyspnea for 3 weeks, beginning 5 months into treatment with bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, procarbazine and prednisone. Chest x-ray shows bibasilar interstitial infiltrates. Sputum and blood cultures are negative, and echocardiography is normal.
oneliner: 24M + Hodgkin lymphoma + 5 mo of combination chemotherapy + dry cough, dyspnea + bibasilar interstitial infiltrates + negative cultures + normal echo → which drug?
ask: Which of his drugs most likely caused these findings?

whyNot.C: Causes **peripheral neuropathy and constipation**, not lung fibrosis
whyNot.E: Main toxicity is **hemorrhagic cystitis**; lung injury is rare

why: **Dry cough + interstitial infiltrates months into chemotherapy + negative cultures** = **bleomycin** pneumonitis and fibrosis. It has **little marrow toxicity**, and lung toxicity rises with dose and oxygen.

drug.name: Bleomycin
drug.how: Generates free radicals that cause DNA strand breaks (G2 phase)
drug.watch: Pulmonary fibrosis, skin hyperpigmentation, minimal myelosuppression

stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic colon cancer receives a combination of fluorouracil, irinotecan and leucovorin. Ten days after his second cycle he has painful mouth ulcers, watery diarrhea, patchy hair thinning, and a neutrophil count of 600/mm3. Liver enzymes, creatinine and mental status are normal.
oneliner: 58M + metastatic colon cancer on 5-FU, irinotecan, leucovorin + 10 d after cycle 2 + mouth ulcers, diarrhea, hair thinning, ANC 600 + normal liver, kidney, mental status → why these organs?
ask: These toxicities share which of the following underlying features?

options.A: Extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism of the drugs
options.B: High renal tubular concentration of the drugs
options.E: Rapid cell turnover in the affected tissues

whyNot.A: Liver enzymes are **normal**; liver toxicity is not the pattern
whyNot.B: Creatinine is **normal**; this would produce nephrotoxicity
whyNot.C: Mental status is **normal**; no neurologic toxicity
whyNot.D: No **immune-mediated** process explains hair, gut and marrow together

answer: Cytotoxic drugs injure rapidly dividing cells (marrow, mucosa, hair follicles)
why: **Mucositis + diarrhea + alopecia + neutropenia** are the signature of cytotoxic chemotherapy: the drugs (**fluorouracil, irinotecan**) hit **rapidly dividing tissues** such as marrow, gut mucosa and hair follicles.

drug.name: Fluorouracil (with irinotecan and leucovorin)
drug.how: Inhibits thymidylate synthase; leucovorin stabilizes the drug-enzyme complex
drug.watch: Myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhea (irinotecan adds cholinergic diarrhea), hand-foot syndrome

stem: A 48-year-old woman with Hodgkin lymphoma receives a single dose of vinblastine as part of a combination regimen. Her physician plans a blood count 2 weeks later and tells her to report any fever.
oneliner: 48F + Hodgkin lymphoma + vinblastine given + blood count planned at 2 wk, report fever → which lab change expected?
ask: Which of the following laboratory changes is most likely at that time?

whyNot.B: Marrow suppression would **lower**, not raise, red cells
whyNot.C: Not a feature of the drug; coagulation factors are unaffected
whyNot.D: Reflects **iron deficiency**, not a chemotherapy effect
whyNot.E: Not the dose-limiting effect of the drug

why: **Vinblastine** is the vinca alkaloid whose dose-limiting toxicity is **myelosuppression**; neutrophils reach their lowest level at about **1 to 2 weeks**. (Vincristine is the one that causes neuropathy.)

drug.name: Vinblastine
drug.how: Binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization (M phase)
drug.use: Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular cancer, Kaposi sarcoma

stem: A 44-year-old man with central nervous system lymphoma receives high-dose intravenous methotrexate. His creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL, so the drug will clear slowly from the blood. A second drug is added to protect his normal marrow and gut cells from the effects of methotrexate.
oneliner: 44M + CNS lymphoma + high-dose IV methotrexate + creatinine 2.3 + second drug added to protect normal cells → which agent?
ask: Which of the following agents is most appropriate?

whyNot.A: **Needs dihydrofolate reductase** to become active, and methotrexate has blocked that enzyme
whyNot.C: Cofactor for **pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase**; no role here
whyNot.D: Used for **isoniazid** toxicity; no role here

why: Methotrexate **blocks dihydrofolate reductase**, so tetrahydrofolate runs out. **Leucovorin is already reduced** and bypasses the block, rescuing normal cells.

drug.name: Leucovorin (folinic acid)
drug.how: Supplies tetrahydrofolate without needing dihydrofolate reductase
drug.use: Rescue after high-dose methotrexate; boosts fluorouracil effect
drug.watch: Can mask B12 deficiency anemia; worsens fluorouracil toxicity

stem: A 38-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receives his fourth cycle of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). Five days later he has gross hematuria and suprapubic discomfort when he urinates. Urine culture is negative, imaging shows no stones, and platelet count and coagulation tests are normal.
oneliner: 38M + lymphoma, cycle 4 of R-CHOP + 5 d later gross hematuria, dysuria + negative urine culture, no stones + normal platelets and coagulation → which drug?
ask: Which of his drugs most likely caused the hematuria?

whyNot.B: Causes **cardiotoxicity** and red urine only from its own pigment
whyNot.D: A **glucocorticoid** with metabolic and bone effects, not bladder injury

why: **Gross hematuria with sterile urine after alkylator chemotherapy** = **hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein**, a toxic metabolite of **cyclophosphamide** excreted in urine. Mesna and hydration prevent it.

drug.name: Cyclophosphamide
drug.how: Prodrug activated by the liver; cross-links DNA
drug.use: Lymphomas, breast cancer, vasculitis, lupus nephritis
drug.watch: Hemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein; give mesna), myelosuppression, bladder cancer, SIADH

stem: A 27-year-old man with a metastatic germ cell tumor starts a regimen of ifosfamide, carboplatin and etoposide. A fourth drug, mesna, is given with each ifosfamide dose.
oneliner: 27M + germ cell tumor + ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide + mesna added to each ifosfamide dose → prevents which adverse effect?
ask: Mesna is given to prevent which of the following adverse effects?

whyNot.A: Seen with **anthracyclines**, which are not in his regimen
whyNot.B: Seen with **bleomycin**, which he is not receiving
whyNot.D: Not a toxicity that mesna addresses
whyNot.E: A risk of **etoposide** and alkylators that mesna does not prevent

why: **Ifosfamide** releases **acrolein** in the urine. **Mesna** is a thiol that **binds acrolein** in the bladder and prevents hemorrhagic cystitis.

drug.name: Mesna
drug.how: Thiol group binds acrolein in the urine
drug.use: Prevents hemorrhagic cystitis from ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide
drug.watch: Nausea, bad taste, rare hypersensitivity; does not protect other organs

stem: A 66-year-old man with bladder cancer has received three cycles of cisplatin. He now has numbness and tingling in both feet and hands. Vibration sense is reduced and ankle reflexes are absent. Strength is normal, there are no muscle fasciculations or atrophy, and plantar responses are flexor.
oneliner: 66M + bladder cancer, 3 cycles of cisplatin + numb, tingling hands and feet + reduced vibration, absent ankle reflexes + normal strength, no fasciculations, flexor plantars → which neural structure?
ask: Damage to which of the following structures best explains his findings?

whyNot.B: Would cause **weakness, atrophy and fasciculations**; none are present
whyNot.C: Would cause **spasticity and a Babinski sign**; plantars are flexor
whyNot.D: Causes **fatigable weakness** with normal sensation and reflexes
whyNot.E: **Motor roots** would cause weakness, not a sensory loss

answer: Dorsal root ganglion neurons (cisplatin sensory neuropathy)
why: **Stocking-glove sensory loss + absent reflexes + normal strength** after cisplatin = injury to **dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons**. Cisplatin also causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

drug.name: Cisplatin
drug.use: Testicular, bladder, ovarian and lung cancers
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, severe emesis; amifostine and hydration are protective

stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV infection has a neutrophil count of 600/mm3 while taking zidovudine-containing antiretroviral therapy. He is given an injection of a growth factor to raise his neutrophil count. Thirty minutes later he develops shortness of breath, flushing, a heart rate of 124/min and a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. Lung examination is clear.
oneliner: 35M + HIV on zidovudine-containing ART + ANC 600 + growth factor injected + 30 min later dyspnea, flushing, tachycardia, hypotension + clear lungs → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs most likely caused this reaction?

whyNot.A: **G-CSF**: its usual effect is bone pain; this first-dose reaction is typical of the other neutrophil factor
whyNot.B: Raises **red cells** and would not be given for neutropenia
whyNot.D: Raises **platelets** and would not be given for neutropenia
whyNot.E: A **topical PDGF** gel for wounds; not injected

why: A neutrophil-raising factor followed within minutes by **dyspnea, flushing, tachycardia and hypotension** is the **first-dose reaction of sargramostim (GM-CSF)**.

drug.name: Sargramostim
drug.how: Stimulates marrow production of granulocytes and monocytes
drug.use: Neutropenia after chemotherapy or marrow transplant
drug.watch: First-dose dyspnea, hypotension and tachycardia; bone pain; capillary leak
